evidence.title: Troubleshooting intrathecal pumps in pain management: A clinical review.
evidence.abstract: Intrathecal drug delivery systems (IDDS), commonly known as pain pumps, have become an increasingly more prevalent method for management of refractory chronic pain, both non-cancer and cancer-related pain. IDDS are generally regarded as safe and reliable, however there is potential for complications leading to clinically significant consequences, such as accidental overdose, withdrawal and neurologic injury. In cases of suspected device malfunction, it is important to have an organized approach to troubleshooting. IDSS are also utilized for intrathecal baclofen therapy, and several prior reviews have focused on algorithms for management of ITB-related pump problems. While there is overlap with existing literature on intrathecal baclofen therapy, the clinical presentation and work-up varies when utilizing opioids and local anesthetics. Therefore, we propose a stepwise framework for troubleshooting intrathecal pump therapy in the setting of non-baclofen medications.

evidence.title: Closed-Loop Extracorporeal Vascular Cleaning by Staged Chemical Dissolution.
evidence.abstract: A closed-loop extracorporeal system for the removal of atherosclerotic plaque from accessible vascular segments by targeted chemical dissolution in a blood-free environment is proposed. The target segment is isolated by balloon occlusion, drained of blood, and connected to an external bypass that maintains distal perfusion. With the treatment zone converted to a sealed saline chamber, concentrated chemical agents, each targeting a specific plaque component, dissolve the atheroma in situ: ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) for calcified deposits, surfactants for the lipid-rich necrotic core, and collagenase for the fibrous cap. The agents are cycled iteratively to penetrate layered plaque, and dissolved material is flushed out under alternating unidirectional flow, with real-time effluent chemistry providing both treatment endpoint and quantitative plaque composition without imaging. The access geometry uses n+1 balloon catheters to isolate arbitrary vessel topologies, from straight segments to bifurcations and higher-order branch points. An iterative protocol interleaves gentle cleaning sessions with pharmacological lipid and calcium mobilization, progressively draining plaque burden from inaccessible microvascular sites toward accessible ones. Six testable predictions are specified for validation in a porcine atherosclerosis model.

evidence.title: Processed EEG Artifacts and Pitfalls: A Narrative Review and a Troubleshooting Mnemonic.
evidence.abstract: Processed electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used for depth of anesthesia monitoring. However, multiple interference sources can distort raw EEG data, leading to misinterpretation of quantitative EEG (qEEG) indices, potentially resulting in insufficient or excessive depth of anesthesia or burst suppression. This review summarizes qEEG interference and artifact sources, as well as some paradoxical effects and pitfalls, reported in the literature. These factors can be categorized into pharmacological, electromagnetic and mechanical, pathophysiological, and model-related sources. When unexpected qEEG values lack an immediately apparent explanation, a structured approach can be valuable, particularly in complex circumstances. We provide a relatable mnemonic "ANESTHESIA" for troubleshooting potential interference sources. If artifact removal is impractical, this should be acknowledged when adjusting the anesthetic management plan. A systematic approach to identify qEEG artifacts and acknowledge potential pitfalls may improve the reliability of depth of anesthesia monitoring, ultimately enhancing patient safety.

evidence.title: Selected Large-Animal Models of Ventricular Arrhythmias.
evidence.abstract: Ventricular arrhythmias are among the most life-threatening cardiac rhythm disturbances. Owing to their complex pathophysiology and high mortality risk, they remain a major focus of research aimed at elucidating underlying mechanisms and improving prevention and therapeutic strategies. In this context, animal models-particularly large-animal models-are of pivotal importance because they more closely recapitulate human cardiac anatomy and electrophysiology. The most commonly used species include dogs, cats, pigs, sheep and goats. Dogs have historically played a prominent role in ventricular arrhythmia research; however, their use is increasingly constrained by legal regulations and ethical-societal considerations. Sheep and goats, although employed less frequently, have also contributed meaningfully to advances in the field. Among large-animal models, swine are regarded as especially promising, largely due to the similarity between porcine and human hearts and the feasibility of reliably inducing ventricular arrhythmias, particularly under conditions of acute ischemia associated with coronary artery occlusion. Large-animal models are also indispensable for the preclinical evaluation of novel drugs, therapeutic approaches, and medical devices prior to translation into human studies. In this article, we review selected investigations employing large-animal models of ventricular arrhythmias, with particular emphasis on the materials and methods reported in the cited literature.

evidence.title: Hepatic Arterial Infusion Chemotherapy for Advanced Hepatocellular Carcinoma in the Era of Systemic Therapies (2020-2025).
evidence.abstract: Background Management of advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has evolved rapidly in recent years. Following the publication of the IMbrave150 study in 2020, which established atezolizumab-bevacizumab as first-line therapy, multiple systemic therapies have been approved and incorporated into global clinical guidelines. However, outcomes remain suboptimal in high-risk cases (e.g., extensive tumor burden, macrovascular invasion). Summary This review examines the role of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) in the context of modern systemic therapy for advanced HCC. A literature search (2020-2025) was conducted employing a PICO framework (Patients: advanced HCC; Intervention: HAIC; Comparison: any or no alternative therapy; Outcomes: efficacy and safety). HAIC is a regional chemotherapy approach delivered via the hepatic artery, allowing high intratumoral drug concentration with manageable systemic toxicity. It is popularly used in East Asia and has demonstrated promising survival benefits in patients with portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT) or large tumors - subgroups where systemic therapies or transarterial chemoembolization frequently fail. HAIC is an integral modality for advanced HCC, especially for patients with extensive liver tumors or PVTT. It provides critical bridge-to-curative options by downsizing tumors and improving systemic treatment effects. To integrate HAIC into global practice, standardization of techniques, patient selection, biomarkers, and confirmatory trials in non-Asian populations is needed. HAIC can change the standard of care by improving outcomes in patient subsets poorly served by current therapies. Key messages Paradigm shift to synergy: HAIC has transitioned from a palliative locoregional tool to a central pillar of "triple therapy" (HAIC + tyrosine kinase inhibitor + immune checkpoint inhibitor), leveraging immunogenic cell death to improve systemic treatment efficacy. warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.

warnings.mechanism: Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough — adversarial model-uncertainty and practical-operation survival are mandatory
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-017: A discovery engine earns trust when it attacks its own successful proof harder than its unsuccessful ideas. Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.lesson: Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Intrathecal drug delivery systems (IDDS), commonly known as pain pumps, have become an increasingly more prevalent method for management of refractory chronic pain, both non-cancer and cancer-related pain. IDDS are generally regarded as safe and reliable, however there is potential for complications leading to clinically significant consequences, such as accidental overdose, withdrawal and neurologic injury. In cases of suspected device malfunction, it is important to have an organized approach to troubleshooting. IDSS are also utilized for intrathecal baclofen therapy, and several prior reviews have focused on algorithms for management of ITB-related pump problems. While there is overlap with existing literature on intrathecal baclofen therapy, the clinical presentation and work-up varies when utilizing opioids and local anesthetics. Therefore, we propose a stepwise framework for troubleshooting intrathecal pump therapy in the setting of non-baclofen medications.

custody_records.raw_content: A closed-loop extracorporeal system for the removal of atherosclerotic plaque from accessible vascular segments by targeted chemical dissolution in a blood-free environment is proposed. The target segment is isolated by balloon occlusion, drained of blood, and connected to an external bypass that maintains distal perfusion. With the treatment zone converted to a sealed saline chamber, concentrated chemical agents, each targeting a specific plaque component, dissolve the atheroma in situ: ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) for calcified deposits, surfactants for the lipid-rich necrotic core, and collagenase for the fibrous cap. The agents are cycled iteratively to penetrate layered plaque, and dissolved material is flushed out under alternating unidirectional flow, with real-time effluent chemistry providing both treatment endpoint and quantitative plaque composition without imaging. The access geometry uses n+1 balloon catheters to isolate arbitrary vessel topologies, from straight segments to bifurcations and higher-order branch points. An iterative protocol interleaves gentle cleaning sessions with pharmacological lipid and calcium mobilization, progressively draining plaque burden from inaccessible microvascular sites toward accessible ones. Six testable predictions are specified for validation in a porcine atherosclerosis model.

custody_records.raw_content: Processed electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used for depth of anesthesia monitoring. However, multiple interference sources can distort raw EEG data, leading to misinterpretation of quantitative EEG (qEEG) indices, potentially resulting in insufficient or excessive depth of anesthesia or burst suppression. This review summarizes qEEG interference and artifact sources, as well as some paradoxical effects and pitfalls, reported in the literature. These factors can be categorized into pharmacological, electromagnetic and mechanical, pathophysiological, and model-related sources. When unexpected qEEG values lack an immediately apparent explanation, a structured approach can be valuable, particularly in complex circumstances. We provide a relatable mnemonic "ANESTHESIA" for troubleshooting potential interference sources. If artifact removal is impractical, this should be acknowledged when adjusting the anesthetic management plan. A systematic approach to identify qEEG artifacts and acknowledge potential pitfalls may improve the reliability of depth of anesthesia monitoring, ultimately enhancing patient safety.

custody_records.raw_content: Ventricular arrhythmias are among the most life-threatening cardiac rhythm disturbances. Owing to their complex pathophysiology and high mortality risk, they remain a major focus of research aimed at elucidating underlying mechanisms and improving prevention and therapeutic strategies. In this context, animal models-particularly large-animal models-are of pivotal importance because they more closely recapitulate human cardiac anatomy and electrophysiology. The most commonly used species include dogs, cats, pigs, sheep and goats. Dogs have historically played a prominent role in ventricular arrhythmia research; however, their use is increasingly constrained by legal regulations and ethical-societal considerations. Sheep and goats, although employed less frequently, have also contributed meaningfully to advances in the field. Among large-animal models, swine are regarded as especially promising, largely due to the similarity between porcine and human hearts and the feasibility of reliably inducing ventricular arrhythmias, particularly under conditions of acute ischemia associated with coronary artery occlusion. Large-animal models are also indispensable for the preclinical evaluation of novel drugs, therapeutic approaches, and medical devices prior to translation into human studies. In this article, we review selected investigations employing large-animal models of ventricular arrhythmias, with particular emphasis on the materials and methods reported in the cited literature.

custody_records.raw_content: Background Management of advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has evolved rapidly in recent years. Following the publication of the IMbrave150 study in 2020, which established atezolizumab-bevacizumab as first-line therapy, multiple systemic therapies have been approved and incorporated into global clinical guidelines. However, outcomes remain suboptimal in high-risk cases (e.g., extensive tumor burden, macrovascular invasion). Summary This review examines the role of hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC) in the context of modern systemic therapy for advanced HCC. A literature search (2020-2025) was conducted employing a PICO framework (Patients: advanced HCC; Intervention: HAIC; Comparison: any or no alternative therapy; Outcomes: efficacy and safety). HAIC is a regional chemotherapy approach delivered via the hepatic artery, allowing high intratumoral drug concentration with manageable systemic toxicity. It is popularly used in East Asia and has demonstrated promising survival benefits in patients with portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT) or large tumors - subgroups where systemic therapies or transarterial chemoembolization frequently fail. HAIC is an integral modality for advanced HCC, especially for patients with extensive liver tumors or PVTT. It provides critical bridge-to-curative options by downsizing tumors and improving systemic treatment effects. To integrate HAIC into global practice, standardization of techniques, patient selection, biomarkers, and confirmatory trials in non-Asian populations is needed. HAIC can change the standard of care by improving outcomes in patient subsets poorly served by current therapies.
